q: In the cash flow statement of a financial enterprise, such as a non-banking finance company, the interest and dividends received by it on the loans and investments made in the course of its business are classified as cash flows from:

options.A: Investing activities, in the same way as for a manufacturing enterprise
options.B: Financing activities, in every case
options.C: No activity, because a finance company has no operations
options.D: Operating activities, since lending and investing in securities are its principal revenue-producing activities

e: For a financial enterprise, lending and investing in securities are its principal revenue-producing activities, so interest and dividends received on loans and investments are operating cash flows under AS-3, not investing flows as for a manufacturing enterprise.

q: An enterprise keeps a deposit with its bank which is pledged as margin for the guarantees issued by the bank and which can be withdrawn only after the guarantees expire. For the purpose of its cash flow statement, this deposit is:

options.A: Not a cash equivalent, because it is not available to meet the short-term cash commitments of the enterprise and is subject to a restriction on its use, a cash equivalent having to be readily available and subject to only an insignificant risk of change in value
options.B: A cash equivalent, because every bank deposit is a cash equivalent
options.C: A part of the inventories of the enterprise
options.D: A long-term borrowing of the enterprise

e: A cash equivalent must be readily available to meet short-term cash commitments and subject to only an insignificant risk of change in value. A deposit pledged as margin and withdrawable only after the guarantees expire is restricted, so it is not a cash equivalent.

q: In connection with the cash flow statement, Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3) encourages an enterprise to disclose, by way of additional information useful to the users:

options.A: The names of the bankers of the enterprise for the next year
options.B: The cash flow expected to be generated in the following year
options.C: The amount of its undrawn borrowing facilities that may be available for future operating activities and for settlement of capital commitments, indicating any restrictions on the use of these facilities
options.D: The personal borrowings of the directors of the enterprise

e: AS-3 encourages disclosure of undrawn borrowing facilities available for future operating activities and settlement of capital commitments, together with any restrictions on their use, as additional information useful to users.

q: A company issues its debentures to its bank merely as collateral security for a loan taken from the bank, no amount being received on the issue of the debentures themselves. In its fund flow statement, the issue of these debentures results in:

options.A: A source of funds equal to the face value of the debentures
options.B: No flow of funds, because no funds are received on the debentures, the loan itself being the source of funds when it is raised
options.C: An application of funds equal to the face value of the debentures
options.D: An increase in the working capital equal to the face value of the debentures

e: Debentures issued merely as collateral security bring in no funds themselves; the loan raised from the bank is the source of funds. Hence the collateral issue causes no flow of funds in the fund flow statement.

q: An enterprise purchases its own debentures in the open market for Rs 92,000, their face value being Rs 1,00,000, and cancels them at once. In its fund flow statement, the application of funds on this account is:

options.A: Rs 1,00,000, being the face value of the debentures cancelled
options.B: Rs 8,000, being the profit made on the cancellation
options.C: Nil, because the debentures were purchased in the market and not redeemed on the due date
options.D: Rs 92,000, being the amount actually paid out for purchasing the debentures

e: Application of funds is the actual cash paid out, not face value or profit on cancellation. The enterprise paid Rs 92,000 to buy its own debentures of face value Rs 1,00,000, so the application is Rs 92,000.

q: In the fund flow statement of a sole-proprietary business, the cash drawings made by the proprietor during the year for his personal use are shown as:

options.A: An application of funds, because funds of the business have been withdrawn for a non-business purpose, like other payments that reduce the long-term funds available to the business
options.B: A source of funds, because the proprietor is the owner of the business
options.C: An operating expense of the business
options.D: No entry at all, because drawings are a personal matter of the proprietor

e: Cash drawings withdraw business funds for the proprietor's personal use, reducing the long-term funds available to the business. They are therefore shown as an application of funds, like other non-business payments.

q: An enterprise sets apart funds for the redemption of its debentures and invests the amount of its sinking fund in outside securities. In its fund flow statement, the purchase of these sinking fund investments is shown as:

options.A: A source of funds, because the investments can be sold later
options.B: No entry at all, because the sinking fund belongs to the debenture holders
options.C: An application of funds, because funds of the enterprise have been employed in acquiring investments, which are non-current assets
options.D: A reduction of the funds from operations of the year

e: Purchasing sinking fund investments employs enterprise funds in acquiring investments, which are non-current assets. It is therefore an application of funds, not a source or a reduction of funds from operations.

q: In a consolidated cash flow statement of a group of companies, the dividends paid by a subsidiary company to its shareholders outside the group, that is, to the non-controlling interests, are classified as cash flows from:

options.A: Operating activities
options.B: Financing activities, being a distribution of returns to one class of the providers of the capital of the group
options.C: Investing activities
options.D: No activity, because the paying company is only a subsidiary

e: Dividends paid to non-controlling interests are a distribution of returns to one class of providers of the group's capital. In a consolidated cash flow statement they are therefore financing cash flows.

q: An enterprise charges in its profit and loss account an expense for share-based payment to its employees, against which shares are to be issued to them later and no cash is paid during the year. In its cash flow statement prepared by the indirect method, this expense is dealt with by:

options.A: Deducting it from the net profit, because it is not a trading expense
options.B: Adding it back to the net profit before tax in arriving at the operating profit before working capital changes, because it is a non-cash charge that has reduced the reported profit without any outflow of cash
options.C: Showing it as a cash outflow under financing activities
options.D: Ignoring it completely at every stage of the statement

e: A share-based payment expense is a non-cash charge: it reduced reported profit but no cash was paid. Under the indirect method it is added back to net profit before tax to arrive at operating profit before working capital changes.

q: An exporter receives the proceeds of an export bill in foreign currency and converts them into rupees at a rate more favourable than the rate at which the sale was recorded, crediting the difference as an exchange gain. In its cash flow statement, the correct treatment is that:

options.A: The exchange gain is shown as a separate cash inflow under financing activities
options.B: Only the amount at which the sale was originally recorded is shown, and the gain is omitted
options.C: The cash inflow is recorded at the rupees actually received on conversion, the exchange gain forming a part of that receipt and not a separate cash flow or a separate reconciling item of the kind used for unrealised restatement differences on cash balances
options.D: The exchange gain is deducted from the opening balance of cash and cash equivalents

e: Cash is recorded at the amount actually received. The exporter received the converted rupees including the favourable exchange difference, so the whole receipt is the inflow; the realised gain is part of it, not a separate cash flow.

q: The shares of a company are forfeited for the non-payment of the calls in arrears on them. At the moment of forfeiture, the effect in the fund flow statement is:

options.A: A source of funds equal to the amount already paid by the defaulting shareholders
options.B: An application of funds equal to the amount of the calls in arrears
options.C: An increase in the working capital equal to the amount paid on the shares
options.D: No flow of funds, because the entry merely cancels the unpaid share capital against the calls in arrears and no cash moves at the time of forfeiture, the cash having been received earlier when it was paid

e: Forfeiture merely cancels unpaid share capital against calls in arrears; no cash moves at that time, the cash having been received earlier when paid. Hence forfeiture itself causes no flow of funds.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise during a year is Rs 10,00,000. Its stock was Rs 1,20,000 at the commencement of the year and Rs 1,50,000 at the end of the year. Its trade creditors were Rs 1,00,000 at the commencement of the year and Rs 1,30,000 at the end of the year, and during the year it received a discount of Rs 20,000 from its suppliers on the amounts payable to them. In a cash flow statement prepared by the direct method, the cash paid to the suppliers during the year is:
e: Purchases = cost of goods sold + closing stock - opening stock = 10,00,000 + 1,50,000 - 1,20,000 = Rs 10,30,000. Cash paid = opening creditors + purchases - discount - closing creditors = 1,00,000 + 10,30,000 - 20,000 - 1,30,000 = Rs 9,80,000.

q: The investments account of an enterprise shows an opening balance of Rs 4,00,000 and a closing balance of Rs 5,20,000. During the year, investments which had cost Rs 1,50,000 were sold for Rs 1,80,000. The amount of investments purchased during the year, to be shown as an application of funds in the fund flow statement, is:
e: Purchases = closing balance + cost of investments sold - opening balance = 5,20,000 + 1,50,000 - 4,00,000 = Rs 2,70,000. This purchase amount is the application of funds; the sale price affects profit, not the cost reconciled here.

q: The fund flow statement of an enterprise for a year shows the following sources of funds: funds from operations Rs 6,00,000, sale of plant Rs 2,00,000 and long-term loan raised Rs 3,00,000. Its applications include purchase of machinery Rs 5,00,000, redemption of debentures Rs 2,50,000 and a net increase in working capital of Rs 1,00,000, besides the dividend paid during the year, which is not stated. The dividend paid during the year is:
e: Total sources = 6,00,000 + 2,00,000 + 3,00,000 = Rs 11,00,000. Known applications = 5,00,000 + 2,50,000 + 1,00,000 = Rs 8,50,000. Dividend paid = 11,00,000 - 8,50,000 = Rs 2,50,000, since sources must equal applications.

q: An enterprise begins a year with its bank overdraft exceeding its cash and other cash equivalents by Rs 30,000, so that its cash and cash equivalents at the commencement are a negative Rs 30,000. During the year, its net cash flow from operating activities is an inflow of Rs 1,50,000, from investing activities an outflow of Rs 1,80,000 and from financing activities an inflow of Rs 80,000. Its cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year are:

options.C: A negative Rs 30,000

e: Closing cash = opening balance + operating inflow - investing outflow + financing inflow = -30,000 + 1,50,000 - 1,80,000 + 80,000 = Rs 20,000.

q: A job can be made on Machine A, whose annual fixed costs are Rs 2,00,000 and variable cost is Rs 30 per unit, or on Machine B, whose annual fixed costs are Rs 3,50,000 and variable cost is Rs 18 per unit. The cost indifference point between the two machines is:

options.A: 7,500 units
options.B: 10,000 units
options.C: 12,500 units
options.D: 15,000 units

e: At the indifference point total costs are equal: 2,00,000 + 30x = 3,50,000 + 18x, so 12x = 1,50,000 and x = 12,500 units. Below this Machine A is cheaper; above it Machine B is cheaper.

q: Philip Crosby's approach to quality management lays down, as the performance standard for quality:

options.A: An acceptable quality level permitting up to 2.5% defective output
options.B: Zero defects
options.C: Not more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities
options.D: Defects of less than 1% of output, checked by full inspection

e: Philip Crosby's quality philosophy sets zero defects as the performance standard - quality is conformance to requirements and defects are not accepted as a permissible percentage of output.

q: A firm purchases 5,000 kg of a material at a list price of Rs 40 per kg, on which a trade discount of 5% is allowed. Freight and transit insurance on the consignment amount to Rs 5,000. The landed cost of the material per kg is:
e: Net price per kg = 40 - 5% of 40 = Rs 38. Landed cost = (5,000 x 38 + 5,000 freight and insurance) / 5,000 = (1,90,000 + 5,000) / 5,000 = Rs 39.00 per kg.

q: Interest on the capital employed in a business is generally NOT recorded in the cost accounts maintained for cost ascertainment, because:

options.A: Interest, whether on borrowed or on own capital, is a financing charge and not an item of production cost
options.B: The amount of interest is always too small to affect the cost of a product
options.C: Interest is payable only out of profits and is therefore a capital receipt
options.D: The Companies Act prohibits the recording of interest in any account book

e: Interest on capital, whether borrowed or own, is a financing charge arising from how the business is financed, not from production. It is therefore generally excluded from cost ascertainment in cost accounts.

q: A machine has an availability rate of 90%, a performance rate of 95% and a quality rate of 98%. Its Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) is:
e: OEE = availability x performance x quality = 0.90 x 0.95 x 0.98 = 0.8379, that is 83.79%.

q: In statistical quality control through control charts, a process is regarded as out of control, calling for a search for assignable (special) causes, when:

options.A: All the plotted points lie close to the central line of the chart
options.B: One or more plotted points fall outside the control limits, or the points show a non-random pattern
options.C: The sample size taken for inspection is increased by the inspector
options.D: The plotted points move up and down within the control limits in a random manner

e: A process is out of control when plotted points fall outside the control limits or show a non-random pattern, indicating assignable or special causes that must be searched for and removed.

q: The observed time for an operation is 12 minutes and the worker's performance rating is 110%. Allowances for rest and contingencies are 15% of the normal time. The standard time for the operation is:

options.A: 12.00 minutes
options.B: 13.20 minutes
options.C: 13.80 minutes
options.D: 15.18 minutes

e: Normal time = observed time x rating = 12 x 110% = 13.20 minutes. Standard time = normal time + 15% allowances = 13.20 x 1.15 = 15.18 minutes.

q: A manufacturer pays GST on raw material purchases and is entitled to full input tax credit of the tax so paid. For costing purposes, the cost of the material purchased will be taken as:

options.A: The invoice price including the GST paid on it
options.B: The invoice price excluding the GST for which input tax credit is available
options.C: The invoice price plus GST, with the GST shown separately as a production overhead
options.D: The invoice price including GST, less cash discount received from the supplier

e: Where full input tax credit is available, GST paid on purchases is recoverable and not a cost of the material. The material is therefore costed at the invoice price excluding that GST.

q: Under Taguchi's quality loss function, the loss at the specification limit, where the deviation from the target value is 0.04 mm, is Rs 128 per unit. The loss for a unit whose deviation from the target is 0.03 mm is:

options.A: Rs 72
options.B: Rs 96
options.C: Rs 128
options.D: Rs 18

e: Taguchi loss varies with the square of deviation: loss = k x deviation squared. k = 128 / (0.04 x 0.04) = 80,000, so loss at 0.03 mm = 80,000 x 0.03 x 0.03 = Rs 72.

q: Work sampling (activity sampling), as a technique of work measurement, is based on:

options.A: Continuous stop-watch timing of one selected worker over a full shift
options.B: Predetermined time values assigned in advance to basic human motions
options.C: Counting the number of units produced by a worker during the period of study
options.D: A large number of random instantaneous observations, from which the proportion of time spent on each activity is statistically estimated

e: Work sampling estimates the proportion of time spent on each activity from a large number of random instantaneous observations, using statistical sampling rather than continuous timing of one worker.

q: A firm can own a delivery vehicle, involving annual fixed costs (depreciation, insurance and taxes) of Rs 3,24,000 and a running cost of Rs 12 per km, or it can hire a vehicle at an all-inclusive charge of Rs 30 per km. Owning the vehicle becomes cheaper than hiring beyond a running of:

options.A: 10,800 km per year
options.B: 27,000 km per year
options.C: 12,000 km per year
options.D: 18,000 km per year

e: Owning costs 3,24,000 + 12x and hiring costs 30x. Setting them equal: 18x = 3,24,000, so x = 18,000 km per year. Beyond this running, owning is cheaper than hiring.

q: Bonus payable to employees under a statute, such as bonus under the Payment of Bonus Act, is treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: An appropriation of profits and therefore excluded from the cost accounts
options.B: A part of the employee (labour) cost of the period
options.C: A selling and distribution overhead of the period
options.D: A charge recorded only in the financial accounts, below the line

e: Statutory bonus payable to employees is a cost of employing labour for the period, not an appropriation of profit. It is therefore treated as part of employee or labour cost in cost accounts.

q: For a possible failure mode of a component, the severity rating is 9, the occurrence rating is 4 and the detection rating is 5. The Risk Priority Number (RPN) under Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) is:
e: Risk Priority Number = severity x occurrence x detection = 9 x 4 x 5 = 180. Higher RPN indicates a failure mode needing priority attention in FMEA.

q: Certification of a company's quality system under ISO 9001 signifies that:

options.A: Every product manufactured by the company is guaranteed to be free from defects
options.B: The products of the company have been approved for export to all countries
options.C: The company's quality management system conforms to the standard; it is not a certification of the quality of any individual product
options.D: The company has adopted Total Quality Management in all its departments

e: ISO 9001 certification attests that the company's quality management system conforms to the standard. It does not certify or guarantee the quality of any individual product.

q: In a Just-in-Time system, the daily demand for a component is 100 units, the replenishment lead time is 2 days, a safety factor of 10% is provided, and each container holds 20 units. Using the formula: number of kanbans = (daily demand x lead time x (1 + safety factor)) / container size, the number of kanban cards required is:
e: Number of kanbans = (daily demand x lead time x (1 + safety factor)) / container size = (100 x 2 x 1.10) / 20 = 220 / 20 = 11 cards.

q: Codification of materials in a stores organisation means:

options.A: Allotting a distinct code number or symbol to each item of material, so that it can be identified unambiguously for receipt, storage, issue and accounting
options.B: Classifying materials into A, B and C categories according to their annual consumption value
options.C: Fixing the maximum, minimum and re-order levels for every item of stores
options.D: Storing every item of material in a bin bearing the name of the supplier

e: Codification allots a distinct code number or symbol to each item of material so it can be identified unambiguously for receipt, storage, issue and accounting. It is not ABC classification or level fixing.

q: A project activity has a normal time of 20 days with a cost of Rs 5,00,000 and a crash time of 14 days with a cost of Rs 5,90,000. The cost slope of the activity is:

options.A: Rs 9,000 per day
options.B: Rs 25,000 per day
options.C: Rs 15,000 per day
options.D: Rs 6,428 per day

e: Cost slope = (crash cost - normal cost) / (normal time - crash time) = (5,90,000 - 5,00,000) / (20 - 14) = 90,000 / 6 = Rs 15,000 per day.

q: Under Total Productive Maintenance (TPM), 'autonomous maintenance' refers to:

options.A: Maintenance of machines carried out entirely by outside contractors
options.B: Routine care and minor maintenance of equipment, such as cleaning, lubrication and inspection, carried out by the machine operators themselves
options.C: Maintenance undertaken only after a machine has broken down completely
options.D: The use of fully automatic machines which require no maintenance at all

e: Under TPM, autonomous maintenance means machine operators themselves carry out routine care and minor maintenance - cleaning, lubrication and inspection - rather than leaving all maintenance to a separate department or contractors.

q: A production line works for 450 minutes of available time per day and the customers' demand is 900 units per day. The takt time for the line is:

options.A: 20 seconds per unit
options.B: 45 seconds per unit
options.C: 30 seconds per unit
options.D: 120 seconds per unit

e: Takt time = available time / customer demand = 450 minutes / 900 units = 0.5 minute per unit = 30 seconds per unit. Production must match this pace to meet demand.

q: Cash discount received from suppliers for prompt payment of material bills is treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: A deduction from the cost of materials, in the same way as trade discount
options.B: A recovery of factory overheads of the period of payment
options.C: A financial income; it is not deducted from the cost of materials
options.D: A deduction from the wages bill of the stores department

e: Cash discount for prompt payment is a financial gain from financing and payment timing, not a reduction in the purchase price like trade discount. It is treated as financial income and not deducted from material cost.

q: A factory carries out 200 set-ups in a year. Through set-up reduction (SMED) techniques, the set-up time is brought down from 3 hours to 45 minutes per set-up. The production time released in a year by this reduction is:

options.A: 150 hours
options.B: 225 hours
options.C: 600 hours
options.D: 450 hours

e: Time saved per set-up = 3 hours - 0.75 hour = 2.25 hours. For 200 set-ups, production time released = 200 x 2.25 = 450 hours per year.

q: The Deming cycle (PDCA) of continuous improvement consists of the four stages of:

options.A: Plan, Do, Check and Act
options.B: Prepare, Develop, Control and Apply
options.C: Plan, Organise, Direct and Control
options.D: Predict, Design, Check and Analyse

e: The Deming PDCA cycle consists of Plan, Do, Check and Act: plan a change, carry it out, check the results, and act to standardise or improve, repeating the cycle continuously.

q: A component has specification limits of 10.60 mm (upper) and 9.40 mm (lower). The process mean is 10.10 mm and the process standard deviation is 0.10 mm. The process capability index Cpk, being the smaller of (USL - mean)/3 sigma and (mean - LSL)/3 sigma, is:
'Variety reduction', as a measure of stores control, aims at:

options.A: Reducing the quantity held of every item of stores below its re-order level
options.B: Classifying stores items according to their annual consumption value for selective control
options.C: Reducing the number of different items, sizes and specifications held in stock through standardisation, so that the total inventory and its cost come down
options.D: Disposing of all slow-moving items in the stores immediately, at whatever price they fetch

e: Variety reduction cuts the number of different items, sizes and specifications held through standardisation. Fewer varieties reduce total inventory, handling and obsolescence cost.

q: A diesel locomotive consumes 4,800 litres of fuel in performing 9,60,000 gross tonne-kilometres (GTKM) of work. The specific fuel consumption, expressed in litres per 1,000 GTKM, is:

options.A: 0.5 litres
options.B: 4.8 litres
options.C: 50 litres
options.D: 5.0 litres

e: Specific fuel consumption = 4,800 litres / (9,60,000 / 1,000) GTKM = 4,800 / 960 = 5.0 litres per 1,000 GTKM.

q: At the Six Sigma level of quality performance, the expected rate of defects is:

options.A: About 3.4 defects per million opportunities
options.B: Zero defects in every million opportunities, without exception
options.C: About 3.4 defects per thousand opportunities
options.D: About 34 defects per million opportunities

e: Six Sigma performance corresponds to about 3.4 defects per million opportunities, allowing for a 1.5 sigma shift in the process mean over the long term.

q: An item of closing stock cost Rs 1,50,000. It is expected to be sold for Rs 1,42,000, and costs of Rs 12,000 will have to be incurred to complete and sell it. The value at which the item will be carried in the accounts, being the lower of cost and net realisable value, is:
e: Net realisable value = expected selling price - costs to complete and sell = 1,42,000 - 12,000 = Rs 1,30,000. Stock is carried at the lower of cost Rs 1,50,000 and NRV, so Rs 1,30,000.

q: Retrenchment compensation paid to workers on the permanent discontinuance of a product line is treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: A direct labour cost of the last batch produced on that line
options.B: A factory overhead to be spread over the remaining products of the factory
options.C: A selling expense of the period in which the line is closed
options.D: An abnormal item, excluded from the cost of products and written off to the Costing Profit and Loss Account

e: Retrenchment compensation on permanent discontinuance of a product line is an abnormal, non-recurring item unrelated to normal production. It is excluded from product costs and written off to the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

q: A firm sets apart a profit-sharing bonus pool of Rs 2,40,000, to be distributed among the workers in proportion to the wages earned by each of them. The total wages bill of the eligible workers is Rs 48,00,000. The share of a worker who earned wages of Rs 72,000 during the year is:
e: Worker's share = pool x worker's wages / total wages = 2,40,000 x 72,000 / 48,00,000 = 2,40,000 x 0.015 = Rs 3,600.

q: The cause-and-effect diagram developed by Kaoru Ishikawa, popularly called the 'fishbone' diagram, is used in quality management to:

options.A: Plot sample results against upper and lower control limits
options.B: Rank the causes of defects in the descending order of their frequency
options.C: Systematically identify and organise the possible causes of a quality problem under heads such as men, machines, materials and methods
options.D: Compute the capability index of a production process

e: Ishikawa's fishbone or cause-and-effect diagram systematically organises possible causes of a quality problem under heads such as men, machines, materials and methods, so root causes can be identified.

q: In a production cycle of 16 hours for a batch, the actual processing (value-adding) time is 6 hours, inspection takes 1 hour, moving takes 1 hour and waiting and storage account for 8 hours. The manufacturing cycle efficiency is:
e: Manufacturing cycle efficiency = value-adding processing time / total cycle time = 6 / 16 = 0.375, that is 37.5%. Inspection, moving, waiting and storage are non-value-adding time.

q: A supplier charges Rs 500 for each returnable container in which materials are supplied, but allows a credit of only Rs 420 when the container is returned in good condition. In the buyer's cost accounts, the difference of Rs 80 per container represents:

options.A: A cash discount earned on the purchase of materials
options.B: An abnormal loss to be written off to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.C: A reduction in the invoice price of the materials purchased
options.D: A hire and wear charge on containers, forming part of the cost of the materials purchased

e: The supplier charges Rs 500 but credits only Rs 420 on return, so Rs 80 per container is retained for hire and wear. This charge forms part of the cost of the materials purchased in the buyer's cost accounts.

q: A factory schedules 25,000 man-days of work during a year, but 1,250 man-days are lost through absenteeism. The rate of absenteeism is:
e: Absenteeism rate = man-days lost / man-days scheduled x 100 = 1,250 / 25,000 x 100 = 5.00%.

q: Quality Function Deployment (QFD) is a technique which:

options.A: Translates the requirements of the customer, the 'voice of the customer', into specific engineering and design characteristics of the product, through a matrix called the House of Quality
options.B: Deploys quality inspectors at every stage of the production line
options.C: Schedules the production of products strictly in the order of customer priority
options.D: Measures the rate of defects in the finished products of a factory

e: Quality Function Deployment translates the voice of the customer into specific engineering and design characteristics through the House of Quality matrix, linking customer requirements to technical requirements.

q: The total cost of production of a factory for a period is Rs 7,50,000 and 10,000 units are produced during the period. If the closing stock of finished goods is 1,500 units, valued at cost of production, the value of the closing stock is:

options.A: Rs 75

e: Cost per unit = 7,50,000 / 10,000 = Rs 75. Closing stock of 1,500 units at cost of production = 1,500 x 75 = Rs 1,12,500.

q: Under a vendor-managed inventory (VMI) arrangement between a buyer and a supplier:

options.A: The buyer inspects and approves every consignment at the supplier's works before it is despatched
options.B: The supplier monitors the buyer's stock levels and usage data and itself decides and effects replenishment, without the buyer placing routine purchase orders
options.C: The goods stored at the buyer's premises continue to be insured and financed by the buyer from the date of delivery
options.D: The buyer prepares the production schedule of the supplier for the whole year in advance

e: Under vendor-managed inventory, the supplier monitors the buyer's stock levels and usage data and itself decides and effects replenishment, without the buyer placing routine purchase orders for each replenishment.

q: A finished product passes through Process I, in which 20% of the input is lost, and then through Process II, in which 10% of its input is lost. To obtain a final output of 7,200 units, the number of units of raw material that must be introduced into Process I is:

options.A: 8,000 units
options.B: 9,000 units
options.C: 9,216 units
options.D: 10,000 units

e: Overall yield = (1 - 0.20) x (1 - 0.10) = 0.80 x 0.90 = 0.72. Input required = final output / yield = 7,200 / 0.72 = 10,000 units into Process I.

q: The Japanese '5S' system, used in lean and well-organised workplaces, is primarily concerned with:

options.A: The five sources from which production waste arises in a factory
options.B: Workplace organisation and cleanliness — sorting out, setting in order, shining, standardising and sustaining the discipline
options.C: The five statistical tools used for the control of quality
options.D: The five levels at which stocks are fixed for an item of stores

e: The 5S system is about workplace organisation and cleanliness: sorting out, setting in order, shining, standardising and sustaining the discipline, forming the base for lean working.

q: A factory incurs a total production cost of Rs 9,20,000 in producing 10,000 units. On final inspection, 800 units are rejected as defective and are scrapped, realising nothing. The cost per good unit produced is:
e: Good units = 10,000 - 800 rejected = 9,200. Cost per good unit = total production cost / good units = 9,20,000 / 9,200 = Rs 100.00, the scrapped units realising nothing.

q: In lean production, the Japanese term 'muda' denotes:

options.A: A signal card which authorises the production or movement of materials
options.B: A mistake-proofing device fitted to a machine or a process
options.C: The programme of continuous, gradual improvement in all activities
options.D: Any activity which consumes resources but adds no value for the customer, such as waiting, overproduction and unnecessary movement

e: Muda is any activity that consumes resources but adds no value for the customer, such as waiting, overproduction, unnecessary movement and excess stock - the waste lean production seeks to eliminate.

q: Five machines together run for a total of 12,000 machine-hours during a period, in which 24 breakdown failures are recorded. The mean time between failures (MTBF) of the machines is:

options.A: 50 hours
options.B: 250 hours
options.C: 500 hours
options.D: 2,400 hours

e: MTBF = total running time / number of failures = 12,000 machine-hours / 24 failures = 500 hours per failure.

q: For inexpensive items which fail suddenly and completely in use, such as electric lamps, a policy of 'group replacement' means:

options.A: Replacing an item only when every item in the group has failed
options.B: Purchasing the items in bulk groups so as to earn a quantity discount
options.C: Replacing all the items of the group together at fixed intervals, in addition to replacing individual failures as they occur, because replacement in bulk is cheaper per item
options.D: Grouping the items together for the purpose of ABC analysis of stores

e: Group replacement means replacing all items of a group together at fixed intervals, besides replacing individual failures as they occur, because bulk replacement is cheaper per item for inexpensive items that fail suddenly and completely.

q: A component can be made in the factory at a variable cost of Rs 45 per unit, besides which specific fixed costs of Rs 80,000 would be incurred, or it can be bought from outside at Rs 65 per unit. The quantity at which the firm would be indifferent between making and buying the component is:

options.A: 1,231 units
options.B: 1,778 units
options.C: 8,000 units
options.D: 4,000 units

e: Making costs 45x + 80,000 and buying costs 65x. At indifference: 65x - 45x = 80,000, so 20x = 80,000 and x = 4,000 units. Above this, making is cheaper.

q: Computer-Integrated Manufacturing (CIM) refers to:

options.A: The use of computer-controlled (CNC) machines on the shop floor of a factory
options.B: The integration, through computers, of the design, planning, production and business functions of a manufacturing enterprise into a single system
options.C: The computerisation of the payroll and personnel records of an enterprise
options.D: The replacement of all manual workers in a factory by industrial robots

e: Computer-Integrated Manufacturing integrates, through computers, the design, planning, production and business functions of a manufacturing enterprise into a single system - more than just CNC machines on the shop floor.

q: Concurrent (simultaneous) engineering, as applied to the development of a new product, means:

options.A: That two competing design teams prepare rival designs of the same product at the same time
options.B: That the design of the product and the design of the process for manufacturing it are carried out in parallel by a cross-functional team, instead of one after the other, so that development time is shortened and later design changes are avoided
options.C: That engineering changes are introduced on the product only after its production has begun
options.D: That the entire design work of the enterprise is entrusted to an outside engineering firm

e: Concurrent engineering carries out product design and manufacturing process design in parallel by a cross-functional team, instead of sequentially, shortening development time and avoiding later design changes.

q: A sum invested at 10% per annum compound interest grows from Rs 4,00,000 to Rs 5,32,400. The compound value factors at 10% are: 1 year 1.100, 2 years 1.210, 3 years 1.331 and 4 years 1.464. The period for which the sum was invested is:

options.A: 2 years
options.B: 3 years
options.C: 4 years
options.D: 5 years

e: Growth factor = 5,32,400 / 4,00,000 = 1.331, which matches the given 10% compound factor for 3 years (1.331). The sum was therefore invested for 3 years.

q: The real rate of return required on a project is 8% per annum and the expected rate of inflation is 5% per annum. The nominal (money) rate of return that should be required, computed as (1.08 x 1.05) - 1, is:
e: Nominal rate = (1 + real rate) x (1 + inflation) - 1 = (1.08 x 1.05) - 1 = 1.134 - 1 = 13.40%. Simply adding 8% and 5% would ignore compounding of inflation on the real return.

q: Two capital projects are described as independent of each other when:

options.A: The acceptance of one does not affect the cash flows of, or the decision on, the other
options.B: They compete with each other for the same site and facilities
options.C: Only one of them can be accepted, the other being automatically rejected
options.D: They have exactly the same economic life and the same outlay

e: Projects are independent when acceptance of one does not affect the cash flows of, or the decision on, the other. They can each be judged on their own merits, unlike mutually exclusive projects.

q: A project is said to have a conventional pattern of cash flows when:

options.A: Its cash inflows are the same in every year of its life
options.B: It requires no initial outlay by the enterprise
options.C: Its internal rate of return is higher than its cost of capital
options.D: Its net cash flow changes sign only once, from an outflow in the initial period to inflows in the later periods

e: A conventional cash flow pattern changes sign only once: an initial outflow followed by inflows in later periods. This pattern normally gives a single internal rate of return.

q: A project will receive Rs 3,00,000 at the end of Year 2 and Rs 2,00,000 at the end of Year 4, and nothing in any other year. At a discount rate of 10%, the discount factors are 0.826 for Year 2 and 0.683 for Year 4. The present value of these receipts is:
In the wider economic appraisal of a public work, benefits that cannot be measured in money terms, such as improved safety and passenger comfort, are properly dealt with by:

options.A: Assigning them an arbitrary money value so that the rate of return can be inflated
options.B: Ignoring them altogether, since only rupee benefits count in any appraisal
options.C: Treating them as a ground for exempting the work from all scrutiny
options.D: Taking them into account qualitatively, alongside the measurable financial return, instead of ignoring them merely because they cannot be valued in rupees

e: Benefits that cannot be measured in money, such as improved safety and passenger comfort, should be taken into account qualitatively alongside the measurable financial return, not ignored or given arbitrary money values.

q: A plant costing Rs 8,00,000 requires working capital of Rs 2,00,000 at the start, which is fully recovered at the end of Year 4. Its net cash inflows are Rs 3,50,000 in Year 1, Rs 3,00,000 in Year 2, Rs 2,50,000 in Year 3 and Rs 2,00,000 in Year 4. At 10%, the discount factors for Years 1 to 4 are 0.909, 0.826, 0.751 and 0.683. The net present value of the project is:

A proposed project will use spare capacity of an existing facility of the enterprise. The capacity would otherwise remain idle and has no alternative use. The amount to be charged to the project for the use of this capacity in its appraisal is:

options.A: Nil, because the capacity has no alternative use and would otherwise remain idle
options.B: A full apportioned share of the fixed costs of the facility
options.C: The rent that a similar facility would command in the market
options.D: A share of the depreciation of the facility based on its book value

e: Opportunity cost governs appraisal: spare capacity with no alternative use and which would otherwise remain idle costs the project nothing, so Nil is charged - not apportioned fixed costs, market rent or depreciation.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 7,58,200, has a life of 5 years with no salvage value, and is appraised at 10%, the annuity factor for 5 years at 10% being 3.791. The uniform annual net cash inflow at which the project just breaks even in net present value terms (NPV = 0) is:
e: Break-even annual inflow = initial outlay / annuity factor = 7,58,200 / 3.791 = Rs 2,00,000 per year, at which the present value of inflows exactly equals the outlay and NPV is zero.

q: An enterprise working under a severe constraint on liquidity may legitimately prefer a project with a shorter payback period to another project with a somewhat higher net present value, because the shorter-payback project:

options.A: Always earns a higher rate of return on the funds invested
options.B: Is exempt from the requirement of financial justification
options.C: Releases the invested funds sooner, for meeting obligations and taking up further works
options.D: Involves no initial outlay in the first year

e: A liquidity-constrained enterprise may prefer a shorter payback because it releases the invested funds sooner for meeting obligations and taking up further works, even if another project has a somewhat higher NPV.

q: A project has an initial outlay of Rs 5,40,000 and uniform annual net cash inflows whose total present value is Rs 6,00,000, giving a net present value of (+) Rs 60,000. The percentage by which the annual inflows could fall before the net present value is wiped out (switching value on inflows) is:
e: Switching value on inflows = NPV / present value of inflows x 100 = 60,000 / 6,00,000 x 100 = 10%. Inflows could fall by 10% before NPV is wiped out.

q: The cash inflows of a project have been estimated in nominal terms, that is, after allowing for expected price rises over the project's life. For consistency, these inflows must be discounted at the:

options.A: Nominal rate of discount, which itself embodies the expected inflation
options.B: Real rate of discount, stripped of inflation
options.C: Risk-free rate of interest
options.D: Rate of inflation itself

e: Nominal cash flows, which already embody expected price rises, must be discounted at the nominal discount rate, which also embodies inflation. Mixing nominal flows with a real rate would be inconsistent.

q: The net cash inflow of a project in a year will be Rs 3,00,000 with probability 0.3, Rs 2,00,000 with probability 0.5, or Rs 1,00,000 with probability 0.2. The expected (probability-weighted) net cash inflow for the year is:
Capital budgeting decisions, once implemented, are generally regarded as difficult to reverse mainly because:

options.A: They are sanctioned by the highest authority of the enterprise
options.B: They involve tax payments in the first year itself
options.C: Large funds stand committed to long-lived assets acquired for a specific purpose, which may fetch little on resale
options.D: They are recorded in a separate capital budget register

e: Capital budgeting decisions are hard to reverse because large funds are committed to long-lived assets acquired for a specific purpose, which may fetch little on resale if the decision is abandoned.

q: A company has 5,00,000 equity shares outstanding, quoted in the market at Rs 84 per share. The market capitalisation of the company is:
e: Market capitalisation = shares outstanding x market price per share = 5,00,000 x 84 = Rs 4,20,00,000.

q: For two mutually exclusive projects, the net present value method and the internal rate of return method give conflicting rankings. The ranking to be followed is that given by the net present value method, because it:

options.A: Is easier to compute than the internal rate of return
options.B: Measures directly the addition to the wealth of the enterprise in absolute money terms
options.C: Always gives the higher percentage return
options.D: Ignores the cost of capital of the enterprise

e: Where NPV and IRR rankings conflict for mutually exclusive projects, NPV prevails because it measures directly the addition to the wealth of the enterprise in absolute money terms, consistent with wealth maximisation.

q: An enterprise has cash and bank balances of Rs 60,000, trade debtors of Rs 1,80,000 and bills receivable of Rs 60,000. Its current liabilities are Rs 4,00,000. Its quick (liquid) ratio is:
e: Quick assets = cash 60,000 + debtors 1,80,000 + bills receivable 60,000 = Rs 3,00,000. Quick ratio = 3,00,000 / 4,00,000 = 0.75 : 1. Stock and prepaid expenses are excluded from quick assets.

q: In discounted cash flow appraisal, the cash flows of a project are ordinarily estimated after providing for tax, because:

options.A: Tax payments are actual cash outflows of the project and must be reckoned like other outflows
options.B: The depreciation charged in the accounts is itself a tax item
options.C: Projects are exempt from tax in the first year of operation
options.D: The discount rate is always quoted net of tax by the market

e: Project cash flows are estimated after tax because tax payments are actual cash outflows of the project and must be reckoned like other outflows in discounted cash flow appraisal.

q: The outside liabilities of an enterprise total Rs 7,20,000, against total assets of Rs 18,00,000. Its debt ratio (total outside liabilities divided by total assets) is:
e: Debt ratio = total outside liabilities / total assets = 7,20,000 / 18,00,000 = 0.40. The remaining 0.60 of assets is financed by proprietors' funds.

q: The year-end convention followed in discounted cash flow calculations is the assumption that:

options.A: All projects of an enterprise begin on the first day of the financial year
options.B: Cash flows are spread evenly over every month of the year
options.C: Tax on project income is payable on the last day of the year
options.D: The net cash flows of each year arise at the end of that year, even though in practice they accrue through the year

e: The year-end convention assumes each year's net cash flows arise at the end of that year, even though in practice they accrue through the year. This simplifies discounting using year-end factors.

q: An enterprise reports a profit before interest and tax built up as follows: profit before tax Rs 3,20,000 and interest on long-term debt Rs 80,000. Its capital employed is Rs 20,00,000. Its return on capital employed is:
e: Profit before interest and tax = profit before tax + interest on long-term debt = 3,20,000 + 80,000 = Rs 4,00,000. ROCE = 4,00,000 / 20,00,000 x 100 = 20%.

q: A current ratio far above the level usual in its industry is not necessarily a sign of strength for an enterprise, because it may indicate:

options.A: That the enterprise has no long-term borrowings
options.B: Excessive funds locked up in stock and debtors, that is, an inefficient use of current assets
options.C: That the enterprise has valued its fixed assets too low
options.D: That the enterprise follows a policy of paying its creditors promptly

e: An abnormally high current ratio may indicate excessive funds locked up in stock and debtors - an inefficient use of current assets - rather than strength, besides possibly idle cash.

q: The profit after tax of an enterprise is Rs 2,70,000. Its equity share capital is Rs 8,00,000 and its reserves and surplus are Rs 7,00,000. Its return on equity (profit after tax divided by equity shareholders' funds) is:
e: Equity shareholders' funds = 8,00,000 + 7,00,000 = Rs 15,00,000. Return on equity = 2,70,000 / 15,00,000 x 100 = 18%.

q: In the mathematics of project appraisal, an annuity is:

options.A: A single sum receivable at the end of the life of a project
options.B: A series of equal cash flows occurring at equal intervals of time
options.C: A fund built up to redeem the debentures of an enterprise
options.D: A payment made once a year towards the rent of a leased asset

e: An annuity is a series of equal cash flows occurring at equal intervals of time, such as equal annual inflows; its present value is found using the annuity discount factor.

q: The net sales of an enterprise are Rs 25,00,000. Its cost of goods sold is Rs 17,00,000 and its operating expenses are Rs 3,50,000. Its operating profit for the year is:
e: Operating profit = net sales - cost of goods sold - operating expenses = 25,00,000 - 17,00,000 - 3,50,000 = Rs 4,50,000.

q: Market value (market test) ratios of an enterprise are the ratios that:

options.A: Relate the market price of its share to its earnings, dividend or book value per share
options.B: Relate its current assets to its current liabilities
options.C: Relate its total debt to its total assets
options.D: Relate its sales to the assets employed in the business

e: Market value or market test ratios relate the market price of a share to its earnings, dividend or book value per share, showing how the market values the enterprise.

q: The inventory turnover ratio of an enterprise is 6 times. Reckoning a year of 360 days, the average number of days for which inventory is held is:

options.A: 30 days
options.B: 45 days
options.C: 60 days
options.D: 72 days

e: Average days inventory is held = 360 / inventory turnover = 360 / 6 = 60 days.

q: The book value per share of a company, as computed from its balance sheet, may differ materially from the market price of the share mainly because the book value:

options.A: Includes the preference share capital of the company
options.B: Is worked out only at the end of the financial year
options.C: Is expressed in rupees per share
options.D: Rests on assets recorded at historical cost less depreciation, and not on their current market values

e: Book value per share rests on assets recorded at historical cost less depreciation, not on current market values, so it may differ materially from the market price of the share.

q: The net sales of an enterprise are Rs 45,00,000 and its fixed assets turnover ratio is 3.75 times. Its net fixed assets are:
e: Net fixed assets = net sales / fixed assets turnover = 45,00,000 / 3.75 = Rs 12,00,000.

q: An analyst finds that the quick ratio reported by an enterprise is higher than its current ratio for the same date. This indicates an error in the computation, because:

options.A: The quick ratio is always reckoned on average balances
options.B: Quick assets are a part of current assets, so the quick ratio cannot exceed the current ratio when the denominator is the same
options.C: The current ratio is always reckoned before the quick ratio
options.D: Prepaid expenses are included in quick assets

e: Quick assets are a subset of current assets, so with the same current liabilities as denominator the quick ratio cannot exceed the current ratio. A higher quick ratio therefore indicates a computation error.

q: The gross profit of an enterprise for a year is Rs 4,50,000 and its gross profit ratio is 30%. Its net sales for the year are:
e: Net sales = gross profit / gross profit ratio = 4,50,000 / 30% = 4,50,000 / 0.30 = Rs 15,00,000.

q: A recognised limitation of ratio analysis is that the ratios, being computed from financial statements, take no account of:

options.A: Qualitative factors such as the quality of management and industrial relations
options.B: The size of the enterprise in absolute terms
options.C: The accounting period to which the statements relate
options.D: The distinction between current and non-current items

e: Ratios computed from financial statements are quantitative and take no account of qualitative factors such as the quality of management and industrial relations, a recognised limitation of ratio analysis.

q: The profit after tax of an enterprise is Rs 3,30,000. Its total assets were Rs 22,00,000 at the beginning of the year and Rs 28,00,000 at the end of the year. Its return on total assets, computed on the average total assets, is:
The so-called ideal or standard ratios used in textbooks for judging an enterprise are best regarded as:

options.A: Rules laid down in the Companies Act for all enterprises
options.B: Ratios prescribed by the lending banks for every borrower
options.C: Broad guides or rules of thumb only, since a suitable ratio varies with the nature of the industry and the enterprise
options.D: Ratios that every well-managed enterprise must attain

e: Textbook ideal or standard ratios are only broad guides or rules of thumb, because a suitable ratio varies with the nature of the industry and the enterprise; they are not statutory requirements.

q: The proprietary ratio of an enterprise is 0.40. Its debt-equity ratio, reckoned as total outside liabilities divided by proprietors' funds, is:
e: Proprietary ratio 0.40 means proprietors' funds are 40% of total funds, so outside liabilities are 60%. Debt-equity ratio = 60 / 40 = 1.50 : 1.

q: The debt-equity ratio of an enterprise is consulted primarily to judge its:

options.A: Ability to pay its trade creditors on the due dates
options.B: Efficiency in collecting its trade debtors
options.C: Profitability in relation to its sales
options.D: Long-term solvency and the relative stake of outsiders and owners in its financing

e: The debt-equity ratio shows the relative stake of outsiders and owners in financing, and is consulted primarily to judge long-term solvency and financial risk, not short-term creditor payment or profitability.

q: A company earns Rs 18 per share and the market capitalises its earnings at 12 times, that is, at a price-earnings ratio of 12. The market price per share implied by this rating is:

options.A: Rs 216
options.C: Rs 30
options.D: Rs 108

e: Market price per share = earnings per share x price-earnings ratio = 18 x 12 = Rs 216.

q: The sales of an enterprise in the current year show a trend percentage of 125, the sales in the base year (trend percentage 100) being Rs 8,00,000. The sales in the current year are:
e: Current year sales = base year sales x trend percentage = 8,00,000 x 125% = 8,00,000 x 1.25 = Rs 10,00,000.

q: The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on Rs 4,00,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years is:

options.D: Rs 400

e: For 2 years, compound interest - simple interest = P x (r/100) squared = 4,00,000 x (10/100) x (10/100) = 4,00,000 x 0.01 = Rs 4,000.

q: The analysis that expresses each item of a single year's financial statement as a percentage of a base item of the same statement, in order to study the internal structure of that statement, is called:

options.A: Horizontal analysis
options.B: Trend analysis
options.C: Vertical analysis
options.D: Fund flow analysis

e: Vertical analysis expresses each item of a single year's statement as a percentage of a base item of the same statement, studying its internal structure, unlike horizontal or trend analysis across years.
